clue.text: Part of shoe conforming with others

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the arched upper surface of the foot, and the part of a shoe covering it
second meaning, read as two words: marching in time with everyone else

explanation.surface: Someone describing a shoe component that matches its neighbours.
explanation.walkthrough: Split into two words, the answer is the phrase for keeping pace with the rest of a marching column.
explanation.definitionFit: The arched middle of the foot gives its name to that section of footwear, and the split phrase means keeping in time with a group.

clue.text: None of relay team have set off in this direction

parts.note: no means none, as in 'no money'

indicators.note: the letters that set off each word are those that start it, so only initials are taken

parts.note: the opening letters of these three words

explanation.surface: A relay squad whose members have all failed to start running this way.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a race, but the team's job is only to supply the first letters of three words after NO.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is one of the four compass points, so it names a direction in which one could set off.

clue.text: Where cobbler should stick throughout life

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the proverb says a shoemaker should stick to his last, the foot-shaped block he works on
second meaning: right up to the end, until death

explanation.walkthrough: A last is a cobbler's foot-shaped mould; the proverb 'let the cobbler stick to his last' warns people to keep to what they know.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means until the very end, so loyal or brave throughout one's whole life up to death.

clue.text: Englishmen in Perth rapidly firing gun

wordplay.note: Pom is Australian slang for an English person, and Perth is in Western Australia; plural, so two of them

explanation.surface: English visitors in an Australian city facing a machine gun.
explanation.walkthrough: Pom is Australian slang for a Brit; Perth places us in Australia. The gun was a quick-firing cannon named for the sound it makes.
explanation.definitionFit: The pom-pom was an automatic quick-firing gun, named after the noise of its rapid fire, used in the Boer War and as an anti-aircraft cannon.

clue.text: Collapse under strain, having accepted a freebie

definitions.note: the answer is a noun; 'a freebie' is a noun phrase, so the article comes along

indicators.note: something that has accepted a thing has taken it inside, so one piece is placed within the other

parts.note: to give way is to break or collapse under pressure
taken as written

explanation.surface: A shelf or person buckling under the load after taking a free gift.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'a' before freebie does double duty in the surface only: in the wordplay it is the letter slipped into the phrase for collapsing.
explanation.definitionFit: Something handed out without charge, such as a promotional gift, is called this, exactly as a free item is.

clue.text: When it's very cold, one may look sharp

definitions.text: When it's very cold, one may
definitions.note: a cryptic hint rather than a synonym: in a freeze one may put on ice skates
definitions.meaning: first meaning, literal: when ponds freeze over, people strap on blades to go on the ice

explanation.surface: A wry remark that in a hard frost a person may look smart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Look sharp' seems to be about appearance in the cold; the idiom means hurry, and the literal reading is about skating on ice.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom is British for hurrying up, matching the command to move quickly and get going.

clue.text: Chap with a passion for church architecture

definitions.note: loose: the answer is one particular church building, the clergyman's house

parts.note: Vic is a man's name, standing for any chap
the article, joined on
rage is a passion, a fit of strong feeling

explanation.surface: A man devoted to admiring the design of churches.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With' simply joins the pieces. The definition stretches a little: the answer is a building owned by the church rather than a style.
explanation.definitionFit: A vicarage is the house the Church provides for its parish priest, so it is one example of ecclesiastical building.

clue.text: 'A". for instance, stands for "Auspices"

parts.note: taken as written
e.g. abbreviates exempli gratia, for instance
to stand for is to be, or equal

explanation.surface: A dictionary entry explaining that the letter A abbreviates a word meaning patronage.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue looks like a glossary line about abbreviations, but each part simply supplies letters in order.
explanation.definitionFit: Under the aegis of someone means under their protection or sponsorship, which is the same as under their auspices.

clue.text: A jolly bad fuss about it — Kipling described how it started

indicators.note: 'about' means surrounding, so the word for fuss is placed around the other

parts.note: taken as written
a Jolly is slang for a Royal Marine, RM
ado is a fuss or bother
ill means bad

explanation.surface: A cheerful but awful row about something whose origin Kipling told.
explanation.walkthrough: Jolly is naval slang for a Royal Marine. Kipling's Just So Stories includes 'The Beginning of the Armadilloes', a tale of how the animal came to be.
explanation.definitionFit: Kipling's Just So Stories tell fanciful origins of animals, including one explaining how this armoured creature first came about.

clue.text: "R" for "Reckoning?

parts.note: surface reading: a dictionary or code-book entry glossing a letter
setter's reading: one of the traditional three Rs of schooling, reading, writing and the one about sums, which begins with an R only when spoken

explanation.walkthrough: The three Rs are reading, writing and 'rithmetic; only the first truly starts with R, so the clue asks which R stands for working with numbers.
explanation.definitionFit: Reckoning means calculating, and the school subject of calculating with numbers is the third of the traditional three Rs.

clue.text: For instance, go for disabled quarry
Garden tool has cut round — it helps to put heel in

definitions.text: it helps to put heel in

indicators.note: going round something means surrounding it, so one word wraps the other

parts.note: shorn means cut, as of hair or fleece
a hoe is a long-handled weeding tool

explanation.surface: A gardener's implement trimmed down, and somehow useful for putting a heel in.
explanation.walkthrough: The word for cut is split around the tool, giving S, then the tool, then HORN. The definition describes the curved tool for easing a heel into a tight shoe.
explanation.definitionFit: A curved blade of horn or metal slipped into the back of a shoe lets the wearer's heel slide in easily.

clue.text: Without you, as they say, what's left to settle?

indicators.note: 'without' means lacking, so a letter is taken away from the word it governs

parts.note: residue is what remains after the rest has gone

indicators.note: 'as they say' points to the spoken form of the preceding word, which sounds like a letter

parts.note: the pronoun is pronounced exactly like the letter U

explanation.surface: A wistful question about what is left to settle once a loved one has gone.
explanation.walkthrough: RESIDUE with its U removed gives RESIDE. The surface sounds like a lover's lament, but 'you' is only the letter U.
explanation.definitionFit: To settle somewhere is to make a home there, and to reside is to live in a particular place.

clue.text: Singer, mid-morning, finally got out of bed

indicators.note: something that got out of a place has left it, so a letter is removed from the end of the word that follows

parts.note: a divan is a low couch-bed

indicators.note: 'mid' asks for the middle of the following word, its central letter only

parts.note: the central letter of the seven-letter word

explanation.surface: A late-rising singer who finally got up halfway through the morning.
explanation.walkthrough: DIVAN loses its last letter N, the middle of 'morning'. The surface pictures a prima donna's lie-in, which suits the answer nicely.
explanation.definitionFit: A celebrated female opera singer, a prima donna, is called a diva, so the word means a star vocalist.

clue.text: None the less, corrosion's ruined this medal

indicators.note: something ruined is wrecked, so its letters are broken up and rebuilt
'the less' means that much smaller, so the preceding item is subtracted

parts.note: the word with its possessive S included
O, a zero, stands for none

explanation.surface: Despite everything, rust has spoiled a military decoration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'None the less' reads as 'nevertheless', but here it means minus one O; the apostrophe S counts as a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The Iron Cross is a German military decoration for bravery, first awarded in Prussia in 1813.

clue.text: Sallying out in striking fashion

indicators.note: 'out' suggests the letters are disordered or put out of place, so they are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Troops making a sortie in a dramatic, eye-catching manner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sallying out' reads naturally as a military sortie, but 'out' is what tells you to rework the first word.
explanation.definitionFit: Signal as an adjective means notable or conspicuous, so the adverb means in a remarkable, conspicuous way.

clue.text: Derived from forebears from parts of Lancaster

indicators.note: taking the parts of something and putting them together anew rearranges the whole word

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A family line traced back to parts of the city of Lancaster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Parts of Lancaster' looks like a geographical origin; the city's name is only the letter supply.
explanation.definitionFit: Ancestral means inherited from or relating to one's ancestors, who are one's forebears.

clue.text: Doctor visited Sanders' subordinate

parts.note: to see someone is to visit them, so saw means visited
in Edgar Wallace's Sanders of the River stories, Lieutenant Tibbetts, nicknamed Bones, serves under Sanders

explanation.surface: A medic who called on someone's assistant.
explanation.walkthrough: Sanders is the colonial commissioner hero of Edgar Wallace's Sanders of the River; his young assistant is known as Bones.
explanation.definitionFit: Sawbones is old slang for a surgeon or doctor, from the days when amputation was a common operation.

clue.text: Two coins (one new, one old) this should cover stamp

parts.note: p is the abbreviation for a penny in the new decimal coinage
the Ostmark was the currency of East Germany, gone after reunification

explanation.surface: Someone sorting coins of different ages and deciding which will pay for a postage stamp.
explanation.walkthrough: The two coins are P, the new decimal penny, and the OSTMARK, the old East German mark. The cancellation mark is printed over the stamp on a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The post office cancels a stamp by printing a dated mark across it, so that mark is meant to lie over the stamp.

clue.text: Policeman putting mafioso finally inside prison cell

indicators.note: putting one thing inside another places it within, with 'inside' completing the instruction

parts.note: cop is slang for a police officer

indicators.note: 'finally' asks for the last letter only of the word it follows

parts.note: the closing letter of the word

explanation.surface: An officer locking up a gangster in a jail cell at last.
explanation.walkthrough: COP takes the last letter of mafioso inside it. Coop is old slang for a prison, from the cage chickens are kept in.
explanation.definitionFit: A coop is a small cage for poultry, and by extension slang for a jail or a cramped place of confinement.

clue.text: Pass by the Spanish Church's eastern end

parts.note: el is Spanish for the
the apse is the semicircular recess at the east end of a church

explanation.surface: Walking past the Spanish church's eastern end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pass by' looks like walking past a building; here it describes time going by.
explanation.definitionFit: When time elapses it slips away or goes by, which is how hours and days are said to pass by.

clue.text: Creature once regarded as divine, namely horse

parts.note: sc. abbreviates the Latin scilicet, meaning namely
an Arab is a breed of horse

explanation.surface: Identifying a horse as a once-worshipped animal.
explanation.walkthrough: SC is the scholarly abbreviation for 'namely'. The sacred horse of the surface is a red herring: the creature is a beetle.
explanation.definitionFit: The ancient Egyptians held this dung beetle sacred as a symbol of the sun god Khepri.

clue.text: Steps taken to eliminate salt from cake

indicators.note: eliminating something gets rid of it, so those letters come out of the word

parts.note: a rum baba is a small sponge cake soaked in rum syrup
a salt is a sailor, and AB is an able seaman

explanation.surface: A recipe step for removing salt from a cake mixture.
explanation.walkthrough: Salt here is the old sailor, abbreviated AB, removed from RUMBABA. Steps are dance steps.
explanation.definitionFit: The rumba is a Cuban ballroom dance, so it is a sequence of steps danced to Latin music.

clue.text: Capitalism, anarchism — both hold charm

indicators.note: the two words between them hold the answer inside their letters, running across the comma

parts.note: spans the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A claim that two rival political creeds each have their appeal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charm' looks like attractiveness, as if both ideologies were appealing; it is really a lucky amulet.
explanation.definitionFit: A talisman is an object believed to bring good luck or protect, much as a lucky trinket or amulet does.

clue.text: Plant arbours?

parts.note: surface reading: an instruction to set up garden bowers
setter's reading: arbor is Latin for tree, so these are a genus of plants that are trees, the maples

explanation.walkthrough: Arbor is Latin for tree, so 'arbours' in the plant world are trees; the maple genus is the one meant.
explanation.definitionFit: Acers are the maple genus, so they are trees, which in Latin are called arbores.

clue.text: Wander around city, talking

indicators.note: 'talking' means the word is spoken, so what counts is how it is pronounced

parts.note: the Italian capital, said out loud

explanation.surface: A tourist strolling round a city while chatting.
explanation.definitionFit: To roam is to travel aimlessly over an area, which is what wandering around means.

clue.text: Spy or nark — 'e gets busily involved

definitions.text: Spy or nark — 'e gets busily involved

indicators.note: 'busily' suggests frantic activity, so the letters are stirred into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written, a dropped-aitch 'he'

explanation.surface: A cockney grumble about a snooper who keeps sticking his nose into other people's business.
explanation.walkthrough: Read whole, the clue describes the answer: a spy or informer who busily meddles. A nark is a police informer.
explanation.definitionFit: A nosy parker is a meddlesome busybody, exactly someone who pries like a spy and interferes in others' affairs.

clue.text: Criminal takes two fools in

parts.note: an ass is a fool, and there are two of them
taken as written

explanation.surface: A crook who brings two idiots into the house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Takes ... in' looks like a container, but nothing is put inside anything: the pieces simply run in order.
explanation.definitionFit: A hired killer is a murderer, which certainly makes such a person a lawbreaker of the gravest kind.

clue.text: Join up broken lines, given time

indicators.note: something broken is smashed into pieces, so those letters are reassembled differently

parts.note: taken as written
T is the standard abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Instructions to reconnect damaged lines, with a deadline allowed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Join up' reads like reconnecting the broken lines; it is really signing up for the armed forces.
explanation.definitionFit: To join up is to sign on for military service, and to enlist is to enrol in the armed forces.
